handbooktext-bogpeat: Waterlogged peat with nodules of bog iron. Breaks into peat bricks and one piece of bog iron; it does not drop itself.
handbooktext-till-reddish: Glacial till (moraine) of the last glaciation: unsorted clay, silt, sand, gravel and stones packed hard under the ice. It stands in steep banks and digs slowly; now and then a stone from an erratic boulder comes out.
handbooktext-till-grey: Older glacial till, dense and blue-grey: unsorted clay, silt, sand, gravel and stones packed even harder under an earlier ice sheet. It digs slowly; now and then a stone from an erratic boulder comes out.
handbooktext-silt: Fine, cohesive silt and loess, laid down by water and wind. It holds a vertical wall and is the parent material of the best farmland.
handbooktext-marl-devonian: Soft calcareous clay grading into clayey limestone, from the old Devonian seas. A pickaxe is quickest, but it is soft enough to break without one.
handbooktext-marl-lake: Pale freshwater lime that settled on the floor of former lakes, full of tiny shell fragments. A pickaxe is quickest, but it is soft enough to break without one.
handbooktext-saprolite-felsic: Granite and gneiss rotted in place to a soft, crumbly clay-sand that still shows the rock's grain and veins. Deep under old tropical land.
handbooktext-saprolite-mafic: Basalt and other dark rock weathered in place to a red-brown clay with green relics of the rock.
handbooktext-laterite-mottled: Red and cream mottled clay under ironstone crusts: the iron gathered upward and left pale streaks behind.
handbooktext-laterite-hard: Hard red-brown laterite crust cemented by iron oxides, full of pea-sized nodules. Tropical uplands with a long dry season.
handbooktext-calcrete: Pale lime crust cemented in dry-land soils, nodular and cracked.
handbooktext-loess: Wind-blown yellow-brown dust, soft and porous; it stands in vertical walls and makes the richest farmland.
handbooktext-tephra: Loose volcanic ash, cinders and pumice from nearby eruptions. It runs like gravel.
handbooktext-saltcrust: White salt crust over the mud of a dry salt flat.
handbooktext-gypcrete: Soft crust of gypsum crystals cemented in desert soils and around salt flats.
handbooktext-permafrost-silt: Silt frozen all year round, laced with ice lenses.
handbooktext-permafrost-till: Glacial till frozen all year round, its stones held in ice.
handbooktext-permafrost-sand: Sand frozen all year round and cemented by ice; it stands where loose sand would run.
handbooktext-permafrost-gravel: River and outwash gravel frozen all year round, its pebbles set in ice.
handbooktext-permafrost-clay: Clay frozen all year round, streaked with thin lenses of clear ice.
handbooktext-ooze-calcareous: Soft white mud of tiny shells from the open-ocean floor.
handbooktext-ooze-siliceous: Fine glassy mud of tiny silica skeletons from the cold and deep ocean floor.
handbooktext-colluvium: Unsorted soil and broken rock that has crept and washed down the slope above.
handbooktext-regolith: Broken and loosened rock just below the soil, grading down into solid bedrock.
handbooktext-terrarossa: Red clay left on limestone as it dissolved; thin, in pockets and cracks of the rock.
creative-date-tooltip: Jumps forward to this date (Earth's /earth date). Time only runs forward: a date that has passed means next year's. The days are real dates; each game day covers several.
handbooktext-mineral-chalcopyrite: Brassy yellow copper-iron sulfide, the world's chief copper ore. It tarnishes to iridescent blues and purples.
handbooktext-use-chalcopyrite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for copper.
handbooktext-mineral-tetrahedrite: Steel-grey copper-antimony sulfide that grows as tetrahedral crystals. An old copper ore, often carrying some silver.
handbooktext-use-tetrahedrite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for copper.
handbooktext-mineral-azurite: Deep blue copper carbonate from the weathered zone of copper deposits, usually beside green malachite.
handbooktext-use-azurite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for copper.
handbooktext-mineral-cerussite: White to grey lead carbonate, heavy and brittle, formed where galena weathers.
handbooktext-use-cerussite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for lead.
handbooktext-mineral-vanadinite: Bright red-orange lead vanadate in hexagonal crystals from the oxidised zone of lead deposits.
handbooktext-use-vanadinite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for lead.
handbooktext-mineral-wulfenite: Thin orange-yellow tablets of lead molybdate, found in the oxidised upper parts of lead veins.
handbooktext-use-wulfenite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for lead.
handbooktext-mineral-smithsonite: Zinc carbonate in rounded crusts, white, green or bluish, from the weathered parts of zinc deposits.
handbooktext-use-smithsonite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for zinc.
handbooktext-mineral-hemimorphite: Hydrated zinc silicate in pale blue-green or white crusts and blades, from oxidised zinc deposits.
handbooktext-use-hemimorphite: Crush it with a hammer and smelt the nuggets for zinc.
handbooktext-mineral-sperrylite: Tin-white platinum arsenide, the commonest platinum mineral: very heavy grains in dark igneous rock.
handbooktext-use-sperrylite: Crush it with a hammer. Its platinum melts at 1,770 °C, hotter than any fire here; nothing in this world uses it yet.
handbooktext-mineral-wolframite: Heavy, dark brown to black iron-manganese tungstate in bladed crystals, in quartz veins and greisen around tin granites and in the slate and schist beside them. Tin miners named it the wolf: smelted with tin ore it ate the tin. In the Erzgebirge the name became wolfram, wolf's froth.
handbooktext-use-wolframite: Crush it with a hammer and keep it out of the tin. Its metal, tungsten, melts at 3,422 °C and was first won in 1783; much later it hardened steel and lit lamps. Nothing in this world uses it yet.
handbooktext-mineral-nativeplatinum: Steel-grey grains and small nuggets of platinum alloyed with iron and a little iridium and osmium, 14 to 19 times as heavy as water. It weathers out of dark ultramafic rock and settles in river gravel: in the Urals, in the Chocó rivers of Colombia and at Goodnews Bay in Alaska.
handbooktext-use-nativeplatinum: It melts at 1,770 °C, hotter than any fire here. Goldsmiths on the coast of Ecuador and Colombia heated its grains with gold until they bonded, in the centuries around the turn of the era; Spanish miners later called it platina, little silver, and threw it away as a nuisance in their gold. Nothing in this world uses it yet.
handbooktext-mineral-pyrite: Brassy cubes of iron sulfide, fool's gold, in veins and dark shales.
handbooktext-use-pyrite: Too poor in iron to smelt, but it strikes sparks and grinds to sulfur.
handbooktext-mineral-topaz: Aluminium fluorosilicate, hard and clear, honey-yellow, blue or pink. It crystallises in cavities of granite and pegmatite.
handbooktext-mineral-tourmaline: Striped prisms of boron silicate in every colour, from black schorl to pink-and-green watermelon. Found in granite pegmatites and schist.
handbooktext-mineral-beryl: Hexagonal crystals of beryllium aluminium silicate: pale blue-green aquamarine, and rarely red bixbite. Found in granite pegmatites and schist.
handbooktext-mineral-spinel: Hard octahedra of magnesium aluminium oxide, usually red and long mistaken for ruby. Found in marble and limestone, and in dark igneous rock.
handbooktext-mineral-garnet: Dark red, green or brown rounded crystals of aluminium and iron silicates. Common in schist and gneiss.
handbooktext-mineral-ruby: Red corundum, coloured by a trace of chromium; only diamond is harder. Found in marble and gneiss.
handbooktext-mineral-sapphire: Blue corundum, coloured by iron and titanium; only diamond is harder. Found in basalt and gneiss.
handbooktext-placer: A placer: river or glacial meltwater gravel and sand in which heavy grains of gold, cassiterite or platinum settled out of the current. Placers lie in alluvium and outwash, often on the old channel floor just above bedrock. Digging gives the gravel or sand and a few nuggets; panning it gives more.
handbooktext-mineral-kyanite: Long blue blades of aluminium silicate in mica schist, gneiss and quartzite, grown deep in mountain belts under high pressure: the Scottish Highlands, the Alps, Scandinavia, the Appalachians. It is as hard as steel along the blade and soft across it.
handbooktext-mineral-sillimanite: White to buff fibres and slender prisms of aluminium silicate (fibrolite), grown in gneiss and schist at the hottest grade of mountain building.
handbooktext-mineral-andalusite: Stout pink-brown square prisms of aluminium silicate in slate, phyllite and schist baked beside granite. In chiastolite slate a dark cross shows where the prism is cut across.
handbooktext-use-kyanite: Crush it with a hammer. Fired, it turns to mullite, the needle mineral of high-alumina brick: crushed kyanite takes bauxite's place in refractory bricks.
handbooktext-use-sillimanite: Crush it with a hammer. Fired, it turns to mullite: crushed sillimanite takes bauxite's place in refractory bricks.
handbooktext-use-andalusite: Crush it with a hammer. Fired, it turns to mullite: crushed andalusite takes bauxite's place in refractory bricks.
handbooktext-use-crushed-kyanite: Takes crushed bauxite's place in refractory bricks of every tier.
handbooktext-use-crushed-sillimanite: Takes crushed bauxite's place in refractory bricks of every tier.
handbooktext-use-crushed-andalusite: Takes crushed bauxite's place in refractory bricks of every tier.
handbooktext-use-grog: Fired brick broken up with a hammer. Tempered into clay, it makes fire clay; with fire clay and crushed quartz it makes a plain fireclay refractory brick without bauxite, as kilns and furnaces were lined for centuries.
